unit.title: Weld using gas metal arc welding process (GMAW) – metal inert gas (MIG)

theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: In MIG welding, what is fed through the gun and melted to make the weld?
options: A tungsten rod that stays solid and does not melt
A flux-coated stick electrode held in a holder
A continuous solid wire fed from a spool
A gas jet that melts the metal with a flame

questions.stem: Why is MIG welding called a "semi-automatic" process?
options: The machine feeds the wire, but the welder guides the gun
The machine moves the gun along the joint by itself
The welder feeds the wire by hand from a separate rod
Half of the weld is made with gas, half with flux

questions.stem: Which helmet filter shade range is generally suggested for MIG welding steel at about 100–200 amps?
options: Shade 3 to 4
Shade 5 to 6
Shade 7 to 8
Shade 10 to 13

questions.stem: Why must a MIG welder keep all skin covered, even in the Jamaican heat?
options: Sweat makes the welding wire rust before it is used
The arc's ultraviolet light burns bare skin like sunburn
Bare skin interferes with the shielding gas flow
Covered skin helps the machine keep a steadier arc length

questions.stem: You are about to press the trigger to feed new wire through the gun. What must you do?
options: Point the gun at your hand to feel when the wire comes out
Point the gun away from people and from your own face
Look straight into the nozzle so that you can see the wire arrive
Hold the contact tip with bare fingers to guide the wire

questions.stem: Your welding gloves become wet with sweat while you are working. What should you do?
options: Carry on, as sweat cannot carry electricity
Take the gloves off and weld bare-handed
Turn the voltage up so the heat of the arc dries them out
Change to a dry pair before you carry on welding

questions.stem: Sparks and spatter from MIG welding can travel several metres. Which precaution is right before you start?
options: Clear anything that can burn and keep an extinguisher close
Spray the floor with oil so that sparks slide away
Cover nearby paper and rags with a plastic sheet
Weld facing an open door so the sparks fly outside

questions.stem: Where should the hood of a fume extractor be placed when MIG welding?
options: On the far side of the workshop, pointing at the door
Directly under the work, blowing up through the plate
Close to the arc, drawing fumes away from your face
Behind your head so that it blows fumes past your face

questions.stem: Why must fume extraction or a fan not cause a strong draught across the weld?
options: It can blow the shielding gas away and cause porosity
It can make the wire feed faster than the dial setting
It can switch the welding machine to alternating current
It can cool the helmet lens so that it fogs and cracks

questions.stem: What can happen if you weld galvanised (zinc-coated) steel without removing the coating or using extraction?
options: You may get arc eye even with your helmet down
The wire will stick to the contact tip each time you start
The weld will be stronger than the plate around it
You may get metal fume fever, a flu-like illness

questions.stem: Which shielding gas is normally used for MIG welding aluminium?
options: 100% carbon dioxide (CO2)
Argon mixed with 25% CO2
Pure argon
Oxygen and acetylene

questions.stem: Which shielding gases are normally used to MIG weld mild steel?
options: Pure argon only, the same gas that is used for aluminium
Carbon dioxide, or argon mixed with some carbon dioxide
Oxygen on its own, to make the arc burn hotter
Compressed air taken from the workshop air line

questions.stem: What is the main job of the shielding gas in MIG welding?
options: To cool the gun so that it does not overheat
To add extra metal to the weld pool
To blow spatter off the plate as you weld
To keep air away from the molten weld pool

questions.stem: How should a shielding gas cylinder be kept at the welding station?
options: Upright and chained or strapped so that it cannot fall
Lying flat on the floor so that it cannot roll over
Standing loose in a corner, away from the machine
Leaning against the welding bench beside the hot work

questions.stem: How should you check the gas regulator, hose and fittings for leaks?
options: Hold a lighted match or lighter near each joint
Listen closely and sniff each joint for a smell
Brush leak-detection fluid or soapy water on the joints
Turn the flow to full and feel each joint with your hand

questions.stem: Why are argon and carbon dioxide dangerous if they leak into a small, closed space?
options: They catch fire easily if a spark lands near them
They push out the oxygen, so a person can pass out
They turn into acid when they touch your skin
They make the welding arc far too bright to look at safely

questions.stem: Why does a carbon dioxide regulator sometimes need a heater?
options: As the gas expands it cools and can freeze the regulator
Warm gas gives a much brighter arc and a deeper weld
The heater burns off any oil that is left inside the cylinder
Carbon dioxide only flows when it is above 100 °C

questions.stem: Which gas flow rate is usual for MIG welding steel indoors, in still air?
options: About 1–2 litres per minute
About 3–5 litres per minute
About 50–60 litres per minute
About 10–20 litres per minute

questions.stem: What does the contact tip on a MIG gun do?
options: It sprays the shielding gas around the arc
It passes the welding current into the wire
It cuts the wire to length after each weld
It holds the spool of wire inside the machine

questions.stem: Which contact tip should be fitted when welding with 0.9 mm wire?
options: Any tip that is to hand, as size does not matter
A 1.2 mm tip, so the wire slides through freely
A 0.9 mm tip, the same size as the wire
A 0.6 mm tip, so that it grips the wire tightly

questions.stem: What should you do with the gas supply at the end of the day?
options: Leave the valve open so the gas is ready for the morning
Take the regulator off and leave the cylinder open
Turn the flowmeter to full so the hose empties out
Close the cylinder valve, then bleed off the gas in the hose

questions.stem: Which type of welding power source is normally used for MIG welding?
options: Constant voltage (CV)
Constant current (CC) only
An oxy-acetylene set
A battery charger

questions.stem: Which polarity is normally used for MIG welding with solid steel wire?
options: Direct current electrode negative (DCEN)
Direct current electrode positive (DCEP)
Alternating current (AC)
No polarity, because MIG uses no electric current

questions.stem: Which drive roll groove is normally used for solid steel MIG wire?
options: A U-groove, as used for soft aluminium wire
A knurled groove, as used for flux-cored wire
A V-groove sized to match the wire diameter
A flat roll with no groove at all

questions.stem: What can happen if the drive roll pressure is set much too high?
options: The wire can be squashed and tangle up at the rolls
The shielding gas flow will be cut off by the rolls
The machine will switch from DC to AC by itself
The wire will feed more smoothly with no problems

questions.stem: Why must the spool brake (tension) be set correctly?
options: To make the spool turn faster than the drive rolls can pull
To stop the gas flowing when the trigger is let go
To hold the gun cable straight while you weld
To stop the spool overrunning and wire coming loose

questions.stem: In the wire classification ER70S-6, what does the "S" stand for?
options: Steel
Stainless
Solid
Spray

questions.stem: How should spare spools of MIG wire be stored?
options: Outside the workshop, under a tree for shade
In their packing, in a clean, dry place off the floor
Unwrapped on the floor so that they can breathe
In a bucket of water to stop the wire rusting

questions.stem: On a MIG machine, what mainly controls the welding current (amps)?
options: The gas flow rate
The wire feed speed
The gun's nozzle size
The length of the work lead

questions.stem: What does turning up the voltage mainly change?
options: The arc gets longer and the bead wider and flatter
The wire feeds more slowly and the arc stops
The shielding gas flow increases by itself
The weld gets narrower and taller, with no other change

questions.stem: What is the best way to find starting settings for voltage and wire speed?
options: Copy the settings from any other machine in the shop
Start at full power and turn down until it stops sparking
Use the lowest settings, whatever the plate thickness
Use the chart in the machine, then test on scrap

questions.stem: Which metal transfer mode is used on thin sheet and can be used in all positions?
options: Spray transfer at high current
Rotating spray transfer
Short-circuit (dip) transfer
Globular transfer with large drops

questions.stem: Spray transfer needs high current and an argon-rich gas. Where is it normally used?
options: In the flat position and for horizontal fillets
In the overhead position only
Vertical-down only, on thin sheet
In every position, on sheet thinner than 1 mm

questions.stem: What is "stick-out" (electrode extension) in MIG welding?
options: How far the nozzle sticks out past the gun's handle
How far the work clamp is from the joint
The length of wire between the contact tip and the arc
The amount of weld that sticks up above the plate

questions.stem: What usually happens if the stick-out is made much too long?
options: Deeper penetration and a hotter, much steadier arc
Less current, poor penetration and poor gas cover
The wire melts into the contact tip at once
No change, as stick-out does not affect the weld

questions.stem: Compared with the pull (drag) technique, what does pushing the MIG gun usually give?
options: A narrower, taller bead with deeper penetration
No difference to the shape of the bead or to penetration
A bead covered in slag that must be chipped off
A flatter, wider bead with a little less penetration

questions.stem: For a fillet weld on a tee joint in the horizontal position (2F), what work angle is normally used?
options: About 10° from the bottom plate
About 90°, pointing straight at the upright plate
About 45° between the two plates
Parallel to the joint, along the weld line

questions.stem: Which travel angle is normally used for MIG welding?
options: About 5° to 15° from upright, along the line of the weld
About 60° to 70°, with the gun nearly lying flat
Exactly 90° to the plate, with no lean at all
Any angle, as long as you can see the weld pool well

questions.stem: Where should you look first to find the wire, gas and settings to use for a job?
options: On the label of the last spool used in the shop
On the job drawing and the welding procedure sheet
On the side of the gas cylinder's safety cap
In the old notebook of a trainee from another class last term

questions.stem: Before MIG welding, why must the joint be cleaned to bright metal?
options: So that the weld looks shiny when it is finished
So that the plate weighs less and is easier to lift into place
So that the shielding gas is no longer needed
Rust, oil and paint cause porosity and poor fusion

questions.stem: A MIG weld shows many small holes. Which is a likely cause?
options: The wire feed speed was set exactly as the chart says
The joint was cleaned to bright metal first
Too little gas, a draught or a nozzle full of spatter
The helmet shade was too dark for the current

questions.stem: What is "lack of fusion" (cold lap) in a MIG weld?
options: Weld metal lying on the plate without melting into it
Small gas holes spread over the face of the bead
A crack running along the centre of the bead
Too much heat that melts a hole through the plate

questions.stem: What is "burnback" in MIG welding?
options: The weld burning a hole through thin plate
The wire melting back and fusing to the contact tip
The gas hose catching fire from resting on the hot workpiece
The helmet lens darkening a little too late

questions.stem: Which of these is a sign of a good MIG fillet weld?
options: A tall, ropey bead sitting on top of the plates
Lots of small metal balls stuck to the plate on both sides of the weld
Grey, sooty marks and small holes along the face
Even width, equal legs and smooth blending at the toes

questions.stem: How should you clean spatter from inside the MIG nozzle?
options: Tap the nozzle hard on the bench until it falls out
Leave it, as spatter in the nozzle helps the gas flow
With the machine off, use nozzle pliers or a reamer
Push a screwdriver in while you hold the trigger down

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

When an active gas such as carbon dioxide is used to weld steel, the process is also known by which three-letter name?

What do the letters LEV stand for, in fume control?

Name the gauge used to check the leg length of a fillet weld.
Gas keeps flowing for a short time after the arc stops, to protect the cooling weld. What is this called?
What is the name of the groove melted into the plate along the toe of a weld and left unfilled?

essays.stem: Describe the personal protective equipment (PPE) a MIG welder must wear, and say what each item protects against.
essays.modelAnswer: A welding helmet with a filter of about shade 10 to 13 protects the eyes and face from ultraviolet and infrared light and from spatter; an auto-darkening helmet must be checked before use. Clear safety glasses are worn under the helmet for grinding, wire brushing and chipping. Dry leather gauntlets protect the hands from heat, spatter and electric shock, and are changed if they get wet with sweat. A long-sleeved flame-resistant cotton or leather jacket, buttoned at the neck and cuffs, protects the skin from arc rays, which burn like strong sunburn, and from sparks. Synthetic clothing is not worn because it can melt onto the skin. Long trousers are worn over leather safety boots so that spatter cannot drop in, and the boots protect the feet from falling plate. A cap or hood protects the head and neck. Ear protection is used when grinding, and a respirator where extraction cannot keep the fumes away.
markingPoints: Helmet with a suitable shade (about 10–13) — eyes and face against arc rays and spatter
Clear safety glasses under the helmet for grinding, brushing and chipping
Dry leather gauntlets — heat, spatter and electric shock
Flame-resistant long-sleeved jacket, buttoned, no synthetics — arc burns and sparks
Safety boots with trousers over them; ear protection and respirator as needed

essays.stem: Explain the dangers of the fumes and gases produced by MIG welding, and describe how you would control them in the Centre's workshop.
essays.modelAnswer: MIG welding gives off fume, which is tiny particles of metal and metal oxide, and gases such as ozone and carbon monoxide. The shielding gas itself can also build up. Breathing fume can cause coughing, sore eyes and throat, metal fume fever and, over many years, damage to the lungs and nerves. Galvanised, painted or oily steel gives off extra harmful fumes, and stainless steel fume is especially harmful. Argon and carbon dioxide can collect in a small or low space and push out the air. To control this, weld in a well-ventilated booth and use local exhaust ventilation: place the extractor hood close to the arc so it draws the fume away from your face, but not so strong that it blows away the shielding gas. Keep your head to one side, out of the plume. Remove paint, oil and zinc from the weld area first. Do not weld inside a tank or small closed space. Wear a suitable respirator where extraction is not enough, and follow the safety data sheet, the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules.
markingPoints: Names the hazards: fume particles, gases such as ozone and carbon monoxide, shielding gas build-up
Gives health effects (irritation, metal fume fever, long-term lung damage)
Local exhaust ventilation close to the arc, but not so strong that it disturbs the gas shield
Head out of the plume; coatings, paint and zinc removed first; no closed spaces
Respirator where needed; follows the safety data sheet, maker's instructions and Centre rules

essays.stem: Describe, step by step, how to fit a regulator/flowmeter to a shielding gas cylinder and set the gas flow safely.
essays.modelAnswer: First read the cylinder label to make sure it holds the right gas for the job, such as an argon and carbon dioxide mix for steel. Stand the cylinder upright on the trolley or against a wall and secure it with a chain or strap. Remove the cap and check the valve outlet and the regulator thread for dirt or damage. Never put oil or grease on gas fittings. If the Centre's rules allow, stand to one side and open the valve for a moment to blow out dust, then close it. Fit the correct regulator/flowmeter for that gas and tighten the nut with the correct spanner, without forcing it. Check that the flow adjuster is closed, stand to one side of the regulator, and open the cylinder valve slowly. Brush leak-detection fluid on the joints and look for bubbles. Then press the gas purge button or the trigger and set the flow the procedure gives, usually about 10–20 litres per minute indoors. At the end of the work, close the cylinder valve and bleed the gas from the hose.
markingPoints: Checks the label for the right gas and secures the cylinder upright with a chain or strap
Checks the valve and regulator threads are clean and undamaged; no oil or grease
Fits the correct regulator and tightens it with the correct spanner
Stands to one side, opens the valve slowly and leak-tests with fluid, not a flame
Sets the flow as the procedure says (about 10–20 L/min); closes the valve and bleeds the hose after use

essays.stem: Describe how to load a new spool of solid steel wire into a MIG machine and thread it through to the gun.
essays.modelAnswer: Switch the machine off and isolate it before opening the wire feed cover. Check that the drive rolls have a V-groove of the same size as the wire, for example 0.9 mm, and change them if not. Fit the spool on its hub so that it unwinds in the right direction, and fit the retaining clip or nut. Hold the wire end firmly so that the spool does not spring loose, cut off the bent end cleanly, and push the wire through the inlet guide, over the drive roll and into the gun outlet. Close the pressure arm and set the roll pressure just tight enough to feed without slipping. Lay the gun cable out straight, take off the nozzle and contact tip, then switch on and press the trigger or inch button until the wire comes out of the gun, keeping it pointed away from everyone. Fit a contact tip of the same size as the wire, refit the nozzle and trim the wire to the right stick-out. Finally, set the spool brake so that the spool stops without overrunning.
markingPoints: Machine switched off and isolated before the feeder is opened
Drive roll groove type and size checked to match the wire
Holds the wire end, cuts the bent end, feeds it through the guides and sets roll pressure correctly
Gun cable straight, tip removed, wire inched through with the gun pointed away from people
Correct size contact tip and nozzle refitted, wire trimmed and spool brake set

essays.stem: Explain how wire feed speed and voltage each affect a MIG weld, and describe how you would set them for a new job.
essays.modelAnswer: On a constant-voltage MIG machine the wire feed speed sets the current. More wire speed gives more amps, more heat, more weld metal and deeper penetration; too little gives a small weld with poor fusion. The voltage sets the arc length. Higher voltage gives a longer arc and a wider, flatter bead; too much voltage gives spatter, a harsh arc and possible undercut, and too little makes the wire stub into the plate and gives a high, ropey bead. The two must be in balance: a good short-circuit arc makes a steady crackling sound, like bacon frying. For a new job, check the wire size, the gas and the plate thickness, then take starting settings from the chart in the machine or from the welding procedure. Weld a test bead on scrap of the same thickness, look at the bead and listen to the arc, and change one setting at a time until the bead is even and well fused. Write down the settings that worked.
markingPoints: Wire feed speed controls the current: more speed gives more amps and penetration
Voltage controls arc length and the width and shape of the bead
Effects of too much voltage (spatter, undercut) and too little (stubbing, ropey bead)
Takes starting settings from the chart or procedure for the wire, gas and thickness
Tests on scrap of the same thickness, changes one setting at a time and records the result

essays.stem: Describe how you would make a single-pass MIG fillet weld on a tee joint in the horizontal position (2F), including the gun angles, stick-out and travel.
essays.modelAnswer: Clean both plates to bright metal and tack the upright plate square on the base plate at each end. Set the voltage and wire speed for the plate thickness and test them on scrap. Hold the gun with a work angle of about 45° between the two plates, aimed slightly more at the bottom plate, because the pool tends to sag down onto it. Lean the gun about 5–15° along the joint, usually pushing, and keep a steady stick-out of about 6–12 mm. Start at one end and make sure the arc melts into both plates and the root of the joint. Travel at an even speed so that the bead stays the same size, and keep the pool inside the gas cover. At the end of the run, pause briefly to fill the crater. Then check the weld for equal legs, even ripples and smooth toes, with no undercut on the upright plate, no overlap on the bottom plate and no porosity, and measure it with a fillet gauge.
markingPoints: Plates cleaned and tacked square; settings tested on scrap
Work angle about 45°, aimed slightly more at the bottom plate
Travel angle about 5–15° and a steady stick-out of about 6–12 mm
Even travel speed, fusing into both plates and the root; crater filled at the end
Checks for equal legs and no undercut, overlap or porosity, using a fillet gauge

essays.stem: Explain the difference between short-circuit (dip) transfer and spray transfer, and say when each would be used.
essays.modelAnswer: In short-circuit, or dip, transfer the wire touches the weld pool many times a second. Each touch makes a short circuit that melts off a small drop of metal. It runs at low voltage and current, so it puts little heat into the work. It is used for thin sheet, for root runs and gaps, and for welding in all positions, and it works with carbon dioxide or argon and carbon dioxide mixes. Its weakness is that on thick plate it can give lack of fusion, called cold lap. In spray transfer the voltage and current are much higher, and the wire melts into a fine stream of tiny drops that cross the arc without touching the pool. It needs an argon-rich shielding gas. It gives deep penetration, a smooth bead and little spatter, and it is fast, so it suits thicker plate. Because the pool is large and very fluid, spray is used only in the flat position and for horizontal fillets. Its light and heat are strong, so PPE must be good.
markingPoints: Short-circuit: the wire touches the pool; low voltage and current; low heat
Short-circuit suits thin sheet and all positions, but risks cold lap on thick plate
Spray: high voltage and current, fine drops across the arc, needs an argon-rich gas
Spray: deep penetration, smooth bead, little spatter, suits thicker plate
Spray is limited to the flat position and horizontal fillets

essays.stem: Name four common defects in MIG welds. For each one, give a cause and a way to prevent it.
essays.modelAnswer: Porosity is gas holes in the weld. It is caused by poor gas cover, such as too little flow, a draught, a leak or a nozzle blocked with spatter, or by dirty plate. Prevent it by setting the flow correctly, screening the work from wind and fans, keeping the nozzle clean and cleaning the plate. Lack of fusion, or cold lap, is weld metal lying on the plate without melting in. It is caused by too little heat, letting the pool run ahead of the arc, or a wrong gun angle. Prevent it with correct settings, a steady speed and keeping the arc on the leading edge of the pool. Undercut is a groove at the toe of the weld, caused by too much voltage, travelling too fast or a wrong angle; prevent it with the right voltage and angle. Burn-through is a hole melted through the plate, caused by too much heat on thin metal or too wide a gap. Prevent it with lower settings, a faster speed and a tight fit-up.
markingPoints: Names four real MIG defects (for example porosity, lack of fusion, undercut, burn-through, spatter)
Gives a correct cause for each
Gives a correct way to prevent each
Links the causes to settings, gas cover, cleanliness and technique

essays.stem: Describe the checks and routine care you would carry out on a MIG machine, gun and leads before and after use, and say why they matter.
essays.modelAnswer: Before use, check that the mains cable and plug are undamaged and that the machine has a current test tag if the Centre uses them. Check the gun cable, work lead and clamp for cuts, burns and loose connections, because damaged insulation can give a shock and a poor clamp gives an unsteady arc. Check the gas hose and fittings for cracks and leaks, and that the cylinder is chained. Look at the contact tip: if the hole is worn oval or blocked with spatter, change it for one of the right size. Clean the nozzle and check that the gas holes in the diffuser are clear. Check that the drive rolls are the right type and size and that the wire feeds smoothly. After use, close the cylinder valve, bleed the hose, switch off, clean spatter from the nozzle and tip, and coil the cables neatly off the floor. Report any fault to the instructor and tag the machine out of use until it is repaired.
markingPoints: Checks mains cable, gun cable, work lead and clamp for damage, and says why (shock, poor arc)
Checks the gas hose, fittings and cylinder for leaks and security
Checks contact tip size and wear; cleans the nozzle and diffuser
Checks drive rolls and a smooth wire feed
After use: valve closed and bled, gun cleaned, cables stored; faults reported and tagged

essays.stem: Describe how you would visually inspect a finished MIG fillet weld, and what you would record and report.
essays.modelAnswer: Let the weld cool, remove any loose spatter and look at it in good light. Check the size with a fillet gauge: both legs should be equal and at least the size shown on the drawing. The bead should be an even width and height, with even ripples and smooth blending into both plates at the toes. Look for defects: porosity, which shows as holes; undercut at the toes; overlap, where metal has rolled onto the plate without fusing; cracks, especially in the crater at the end; burn-through on thin sheet; and heavy spatter. Check the start and the end of the weld carefully, because faults are most common there. Check that the parts are still square and to size, because the heat can pull them out of line. Mark any faults with chalk, write down what you found on the inspection sheet with the job number and your name, and report anything outside the drawing or procedure to the instructor before the job goes on.
markingPoints: Measures the leg size with a fillet gauge against the drawing
Checks the bead shape: even width, even ripples, smooth toes
Looks for named defects (porosity, undercut, overlap, cracks, burn-through)
Checks the starts and stops, and that the parts are still square and to size
Marks faults, records the results and reports to the instructor

practical1.title: MIG fillet welds on tee joints in the horizontal position (2F), 6 mm mild steel
practical1.brief: As a group, set up a MIG welding station safely and make fillet welds on tee joints in 6 mm mild steel plate in the horizontal position (2F), using 0.9 mm ER70S-6 wire and an argon and carbon dioxide gas mix. Together, check the machine, cylinder, gun and leads, and set the gas flow. Each member then sets the voltage and wire feed speed, makes a test bead on scrap, and welds one side of a tee joint (one run of about 150 mm) while the assessor watches. The group will need 2 or 3 tee joints. Each member checks their own weld with a fillet gauge, and another member checks it again. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when every member has welded and the area is clean.
materials: 6 pieces of 6 mm mild steel plate, about 150 mm × 75 mm (for 3 tee joints)
Scrap plate of the same thickness for test beads
Argon and carbon dioxide shielding gas mix, with regulator/flowmeter
MIG welding machine with gun and work lead
Fillet weld gauge, try square, wire brush and MIG pliers
Angle grinder with flap disc (for cleaning)
photos: The welding station set up: cylinder chained, extraction in place, every member in full PPE
The flowmeter showing the gas flow set
Plates cleaned to bright metal and tacked square as tee joints
A test bead on scrap, with the settings written beside it
Each member's finished fillet weld, labelled with their name
End view of a joint, showing both legs
The fillet gauge on a finished weld
The work area cleaned, cylinder valve closed and cables coiled
checklist: Wore full PPE correctly throughout, including safety glasses under the helmet
Helped check the machine, gun, leads, cylinder and hose before welding
Set the voltage and wire feed speed from the chart and tested them on scrap
Cleaned the plates and tacked them square, with no gap
Held a work angle of about 45° with a steady travel angle and stick-out
Finished fillet: equal legs to size, even ripples, no undercut, porosity or overlap
Checked the weld with a fillet gauge and recorded the result
Left the station safe: valve closed, hose bled, nozzle cleaned, area tidy
safety: Weld only in a booth or behind screens; warn others before you strike an arc
Keep the cylinder upright and chained; open the valve slowly and stand to one side
Use the fume extraction close to the arc and keep your head out of the plume
Point the gun away from people when feeding wire; keep fingers out of the drive rolls
Remove anything that can burn and keep a fire extinguisher at hand
Treat all metal as hot: use pliers or tongs and mark hot work

practical2.title: Set up a MIG station, then weld butt and lap joints in the flat position on 3 mm steel sheet
practical2.brief: As a group, set up a MIG station from the start under the assessor's eye: fit the regulator/flowmeter to the cylinder, then load a new spool of 0.8 mm ER70S-6 wire and thread it through to the gun. Share the set-up steps so that every member does at least one step and explains it to the assessor. Then each member makes one square-edge butt weld in the flat position (1G) and one lap fillet weld in the flat position (1F) in 3 mm mild steel sheet, each about 150 mm long, using short-circuit transfer, after a test bead on scrap. Each member inspects their own welds and marks any faults with chalk. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group when every member has welded and the area is clean.
materials: 3 mm mild steel sheet: 4 pieces of about 150 mm × 50 mm for each member
A new spool of 0.8 mm ER70S-6 wire
Argon and carbon dioxide gas mix, with regulator/flowmeter
MIG machine with 0.8 mm V-groove drive rolls and 0.8 mm contact tips
Wire cutters, MIG pliers and wire brush
Clamps, try square, steel rule and chalk
photos: Regulator fitted, with leak-detection fluid on the joints
Spool loaded and wire through the drive rolls, machine off and cover open
Wire through the gun, with the correct size contact tip fitted
A butt joint tacked with a small, even gap
Each member's finished butt weld, front and back, labelled with their name
Each member's finished lap weld, labelled with their name
Faults marked in chalk on any weld that has them
The work area cleaned, valve closed and cables coiled
checklist: Did a set-up step correctly (fitting the regulator, or loading or threading the wire) with the machine off
Chose the correct drive roll and contact tip for the wire size
Set the gas flow and tested the settings on scrap
Butt weld: even bead, penetration showing on the back, no burn-through
Lap weld: fused into both pieces, with no undercut on the top edge
Found and named any faults in their own welds
Left the station safe and tidy, with the valve closed and the hose bled
safety: Switch off and isolate the machine before opening the wire feeder
Keep the cylinder chained; check for leaks with fluid, never with a flame
Point the gun away from people when inching wire through
Use extraction close to the arc; keep your head out of the fumes
Remove anything that can burn and keep a fire extinguisher at hand
Thin sheet gets hot quickly: handle it with pliers and mark hot work
